digest: Stop/cancel runtime deviates from SPEC: stop detection accepts message-based errors, provider cancellation accepts 'cancelled'/'timeout', and the poll default and minimum differ from spec. One signal-binding dedupe risk is noted at lower confidence.

findings.title: Stop-error classification falls back to message prefix matching
findings.evidence: isWorkflowStopRequestedError returns true for any Error whose message starts with 'workflow stop requested', even when the name is not WorkflowStopRequested. SPEC S6 says only the error name may classify a stop, and that message content must not be used.
findings.rationale: Any ordinary error whose message happens to start with that prefix, such as a provider or wrapped error that echoes it, is treated as a deliberate stop. The run is then reported as stopped instead of failing with its real diagnostic, which misclassifies the terminal outcome. The spec explicitly forbids this path.
findings.recommendedAction: Compare only error.name === WORKFLOW_STOP_REQUESTED_ERROR_NAME, and remove the startsWith fallback. If legacy errors must still match, use an explicit marker property set by createWorkflowStopRequestedError rather than message text.

findings.title: Provider cancellation allowlist includes 'cancelled' and 'timeout' beyond the spec's three markers
findings.evidence: The string check accepts 'aborted', 'AbortError', 'ABORT_ERR', 'cancelled', and 'timeout'. SPEC C1 allows exactly 'aborted', 'AbortError', and 'ABORT_ERR', and says other provider errors must not be promoted to cancellation. The code comment also says the check is deliberately exact.
findings.rationale: A genuine provider failure reported as error 'timeout' or reason 'cancelled' is classified as user cancellation. That suppresses its diagnostic and can produce a cancelled terminal state for a run that actually failed. Because the spec names exact tokens and the comment says the list is intentionally exact, this widens the classifier beyond its contract.
findings.recommendedAction: Restrict the candidate check to 'aborted', 'AbortError', and 'ABORT_ERR' per C1. If 'timeout' or 'cancelled' must be honored for an existing provider, scope that to the specific adapter and update SPEC C1 explicitly, rather than changing the shared classifier.

findings.title: Stop-watch poll default and minimum deviate from spec S3
findings.evidence: The code uses Math.max(1, options.pollMs ?? 200), so the default is 200ms and the floor is 1ms. SPEC S3 sets the default at 50ms and the floor at 10ms.
findings.rationale: With the default, a stop intent written to disk can take up to about four times longer to abort the in-flight run than the spec allows. Callers passing very small values can also poll far more often than the spec permits, creating disk-read load. Both are runtime-behavior deviations, not only documentation drift.
findings.recommendedAction: Set the default to 50 and the floor to 10 to match S3, and add a test that pins both values. If 200ms is the intended default, update SPEC S3 in the same change so the contract matches the code.

findings.title: Re-binding the same AbortSignal can drop the launch fence early
findings.evidence: Registrations use a Set, so binding the same signal twice stores it once. The first release calls signals.delete(signal), which removes it even though the second binding is still active. SPEC S7 requires that a run's registration persist until the last signal is released.
findings.rationale: If the same foreground signal is bound twice for one run and one owner releases first, the remaining active launch loses its synchronous stop fence, and a later abort may not be seen before dispatch. No in-repo caller binding the same signal twice was found, so the practical likelihood is low.
findings.recommendedAction: Use a reference count per signal, or a token per binding, so release removes only that binding and the entry is deleted when the last binding is gone.

sourceCoverage.evidence: - **S3.** 중지 감시 주기(`pollMs`)의 기본값은 50ms이고, 호출자가 더 작은 값을 주어도 10ms보다

noIssueNotes: S2: createWorkflowStopRequestedError uses the required name and the 'workflow stop requested for <runId>' message format.
S4: the watch path catches disk-read errors as non-stop, and throwIfWorkflowStopRequested lets them propagate, as specified.
S5: dispose() clears the interval, so the timer starts no new reads. A check already in flight may finish, which is acceptable.
C2: each recursion level parses a strictly shorter nested JSON string, so there is no infinite recursion. The parsed !== value guard is redundant but harmless.
C1 exact-match design for AbortError, aborted, and ABORT_ERR matches the spec. The only deviation is the extra tokens noted in the findings.
Not reviewed: src/workflow-terminal.ts (T1-T3) and the store.js readWorkflowStopIntent implementation, which are outside the planned evidence list.
